10731-the-essays-of-arthur-schopenhauer-:
Arthur Schopenhauer's Art of Controversy, translated by T. Bailey Saunders, collects essays drawn from the philosopher's posthumous papers. Its centerpiece teaches the stratagems of debate: how arguments are won, lost, and twisted, beginning with logic and dialectic and moving to the tricks of disputants. Shorter essays on art, beauty, wisdom, genius, and virtue follow.

The papers reached print some years after Schopenhauer's death through his friend and executor Julius Frauenstadt, and later editors added and corrected them. The tone is sharp, witty, and unsparing. Readers get a practical guide to argument, and a taste of a philosopher who loved a good fight.
11883-entertaining-made-easy:
Emily Rose Burt's 1919 handbook, in the Made Easy series, offers plans for parties, showers. Weddings, drawing on material first printed in Woman's Home Companion, The Ladies' Home Journal, and other magazines. Its contents run from a smiles social and an aviation meet to a mock canteen and a progressive march party.

Burt gives decorations, menus, favors, and games for each occasion, including a nut party with a coconut game, a pussy-cat party for children. Summer weddings decked with wild roses or field flowers. The book captures a moment when home entertaining was a craft, with rules for invitations, table settings, and seasonal themes spelled out step by step.
1243-hearts-of-controversy:
Alice Meynell gathers essays on writers who stir dispute: Tennyson, Dickens, Swinburne, and Charlotte and Emily Brontë. She weighs each with a reader's love and a critic's independence, praising what lasts and questioning what fades, in her brief, polished prose.

The essays show Meynell's taste at its sharpest: she defends Tennyson against new detractors and reads Dickens as a man of letters. The book is short and thoughtful. It suits readers who like literary criticism with grace and a mind of its own. Meynell's criticism shows grace, independence, and a mind of its own.
13506-the-story-of-patsy:
Kate Douglas Wiggin tells the story of Patsy, a poor city boy who minds the Kennett baby and longs for a place in school. Patsy climbs frail wooden steps past tin cans and bottles to a landing, where he sits with a dull little baby who will play all day with an old shoe. Dirtier and more sullen than ever, he still hopes for kindness.

A schoolmistress hears his plea: Jim said she never licked boys, turned away neat little girls in white aprons for lack of room, yet made room for dirty boys in torn clothes. Patsy fears he cannot come every day, because he might have fits. Wiggin writes with pity for sorrowful little lives, and with faith that a welcoming school can change them.
14202-little-prudy-s-sister-susy:
Sophie May's Little Prudy's Sister Susy tells of the oldest Parlin girl, though Prudy's troubles keep stealing scenes. Susy keeps secrets, wakes before daylight, celebrates Christmas, earns wings, and faces moral courage, birthday, and farewell. A preface hopes readers will see kindness in God sending slow winter and long nights of pain to little Prudy, teaching gentleness and patience through trouble.

Truth and play tangle in the middle. Susy wonders if Prudy's limping counts as a wrong story, since the child runs well, then limps and grips chairs when she remembers. Mrs. Parlin fears deceit, yet the lameness proves a sad truth, not mere play. A cake theft follows: Dotty cannot reach the chest, so Susy blames Annie, who often said she would steal cake. Susy then excuses missing eel-jumbles with a dog thief, to the Pipers' calm delight. Family fun and moral lessons share every chapter.
14606-and-thus-he-came-a-christmas-fanta:
Cyrus Townsend Brady's 1916 Christmas fantasy, illustrated by Walter B. Everett and dedicated to the memory of Little Betty, retells the coming of Christ in eleven stages. Putnam published the volume in New York and London.

Chapters move from the Baby and the Child through the Friend, the Workman, and the Comforter. They continue through the Burden Bearer to the Thorn Crowned, the Broken-Hearted, the Forgiver of Sins, the Giver of Life, and the Stiller of the Storm. Brady writes in devotional, imaginative prose. The book is a sentimental Christmas meditation, meant for reading aloud in the season.
17176-the-ghost-a-modern-fantasy:
Arnold Bennett's 1907 fantasy, published in Boston in 1911, opens with a narrator eight years older, recalling a clerk at Keith Prowse's who waved away his plea for opera seats. The tale moves from a splendid cousin and the opera to the cry of Alresca, Rosa's summons, a dagger, a vigil by a bier, and a thing in a chair. Trains, steamers, a villa, and a portrait fill the middle chapters.

Bennett mixes ghost story with modern manners, in prose both witty and eerie. The ghost here is less a fright than a fate, tied to love and guilt. Readers who like literary ghost tales will find a stylish, suspenseful novel from a master of Edwardian fiction.
18377-the-arian-controversy:
H. M. Gwatkin, Dixie Professor of Ecclesiastical History at Cambridge, wrote this short history of the Arian controversy for the Epochs of Church History series, edited by Bishop Mandell Creighton. Longmans, Green published the sixth impression in London, New York, Bombay, and Calcutta in 1908. Gwatkin gives students a clear path through a tangled fourth-century dispute about the nature of Christ.

Chapters trace the beginnings of Arianism and the Council of Nicaea. They follow the Eusebian reaction and the Council of Sardica. Later chapters give the victory of Arianism, the reign of Julian, the restored Homoean supremacy, and the fall of Arianism. A chronological table and index close the book, with a list of works for further study. Readers get church history in brief: councils, emperors, and bishops deciding, over generations, what Christians would believe about the Son.
18687-daisy:
Elizabeth Wetherell, the pen name of Susan Warner, tells this girl's life story in her own voice, first published in 1868. Daisy looks back past bright childhood years to the summer she turned ten and became a Christian, a change she calls the golden thread running through all her later life.

Soon after, her father is thrown from his horse and hurt, and Daisy is sent to Magnolia to live with her aunt Gary under a governess. Chapters follow her through school, housekeeping, French dresses, grey coats, and wartime chapters, as she learns obedience, work, and trust. The book reads as a plain, warm memoir of growing up, with faith shaping how its heroine meets each new trial.
21101-pixie-o-shaughnessy:
Patricia Monica de Vere O'Shaughnessy, called Pixie by everyone, grows up in a tumble-down Irish castle with an eccentric family. Her dead mother left money for her schooling. Pixie travels with her father to a girls' school in the London suburbs. There he suddenly sees how shabby she looks and hears her strong Irish brogue.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey follows Pixie as she wins over her schoolmates after early setbacks. The strongest episode comes when Pixie takes the blame for a lost perfume bottle, keeping a promise to the real culprit. She is punished for the deed and for her silence alike.
21553-mr-midshipman-easy:
Jack Easy goes to sea with more wit than sense in Captain Marryat's Mr Midshipman Easy. His father, a failed philosopher, holds that all men are equal by nature. Jack takes that creed aboard a man-of-war, with comic results.

Marryat makes Jack's schooling in the real navy the heart of the tale. Philosophy, as the book jokes, is no cure for toothache, and no guide in a gale. Friends, duels, cruises, and captures shape the lad into an officer. The novel became Marryat's best-loved tale of midshipman life, full of humour drawn from his own service years at sea.
21893-patsy:
Galloway in Scotland is S. R. Crockett's home ground, and Patsy, published in 1912, is a tale of its Castle Raincy. Earl Raincy and his grandson Louis are known to all the country of the Southern Albanach, as the old fragment runs. Chapters bring a maidens' cove, a bothy, a black pearl of Cairn Ferris, and an old feud's end. Patsy, the heroine, has greatness thrust upon her by the tale's middle.

Crockett, author of The Raiders and The Stickit Minister, packs the book with rescues, plots, princes, and rides in the night. A gibbet ring and a lost folks' acre darken the comedy. Patsy herself is held in honor by friend and foe alike. It is Scottish romance in Crockett's full, dialect-rich manner, made for readers who loved his earlier tales.
23363-a-midnight-fantasy:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich set this dreamlike Boston tale on a still June night, just before eleven, as the narrator leaves the Boston Theatre and crosses the Common. Stars shiver in a cold high wind, leaves hang black and still, and gas lamps turn the foliage a tender green.

From that quiet start, the tale slips toward fantasy, as the night streets, lit windows, and lone footfalls stir thoughts of ghosts, love, and days gone by. Aldrich writes the city as a stage, where calm and strangeness sit side by side. Readers who like a tale that hovers between waking and dream will enjoy its mood, its fine city pictures, and its gentle turn toward wonder.
23777-an-essay-on-the-shaking-palsy:
James Parkinson, member of the Royal College of Surgeons, published An Essay on the Shaking Palsy in London in 1817. It is the founding description of the disease now known as Parkinson's disease, written before the condition had any place in medical classification.

Parkinson admits his limits plainly: mere conjecture takes the place of experiment, and analogy stands in for anatomical examination. Yet he traces a disease of long duration, linking its later symptoms to those of its start, and describes sufferers who saw no prospect of escape from its domination. For medical history, this short essay is a landmark of careful clinical observation.
24309-irish-ned-the-winnipeg-newsy:
The Reverend Samuel Fea, rector of St. Peter's, Winnipeg, wrote this boys' story, published in Toronto by William Briggs in 1910. Its hero is Irish Ned, a newsboy of not more than nine, crying his papers on a hot August afternoon at Portage Avenue and Main Street, the busiest corner of busy Winnipeg. His cry rings shrill and clear above traffic: Free Press, Tribune, and Telegram, three for a nickel.

Ned's clothes are patched and his boots worn and gaping, yet neat, clean, and brushed, his straw-red hair combed, his cap pushed back over clear, dark-blue Irish eyes. His face is bright and cheerful, with a shrewdness born of early experience. Readers get a warm tale of a small newsy whose innocence is a choice of good over evil.
24669-little-scenes-for-little-folks-in-:
Published at London by William Darton and Son at one shilling, this tiny primer tells little scenes for little folks in words of not more than two syllables, with coloured engravings. Its stories include going to church, Charles's new boat, and a morning lesson, each told in the simplest words a beginner could read.

The book's rule is its charm: no word longer than two beats, so a child just learning to read can manage every page. Its coloured pictures help the words along. The primer remains a delightful survival of early Victorian teaching, and a model of how little a first reader truly needs.
26015-a-christmas-posy:
Mrs. Molesworth gathers Christmas tales in A Christmas Posy, printed by Macmillan in 1888 with pictures by Walter Crane. Dedicated to twin sisters Julia and Isabel. The book holds Grandmother Dear's old watch, my pink pet, an honest little man, six poor little princesses, Basil's violin, missing bon bons, lost Rollo, and blue dwarfs. A frontispiece shows Sylvia calling her sister to watch grandmother as far as the corner.

Basil's tale turns on a boy who quits his violin and rolls lazily on the lawn, telling his sister Blanche he has given it up. Blanche, eyes wide, cries how sorry mother will be, while Basil calls it rubbish and says mother always let him stop if he liked. Molesworth writes of children, grandmothers, and Christmas gifts with gentle humor and warmth.
26869-the-tale-of-lal-a-fantasy:
Raymond Paton published this fantasy with Brentano's and Chapman and Hall in 1914. An explanation up front warns, on behalf of Ridgwell and Christine, that facts, common sense, and probability have been left out throughout. The children consider those things an old-fashioned survival. A preface then shows Trafalgar Square as four artists paint it, each as he wishes to see it. The range runs from a Japanese night scene of lanterns to a Cubist field of ochre and green.

The tale itself runs in three books: what Ridgwell and Christine declared, what the writer and the Lord Mayor declared, and what the public heard about. A pleasant-faced lion, a golden pavilion, two Dick Whittingtons, and an upsetting newspaper article all figure in it. The children wait and wait for Lal, who has never broken his word before, and wonder why the grown-ups do not understand.
27949-daisy:
Elizabeth Wetherell, author of The Wide, Wide World and Queechy, wrote Daisy, published in London and New York by Ward, Lock and Company. The novel is narrated by Daisy herself, who seeks an excuse for writing her own life and following its thread of present truth and possible glory.

Chapters run from Miss Pinshon and her home through school, French dresses, grey coats, Yankees, and Fort Putnam, to entered for the war. Daisy's story turns at ten, when she becomes a Christian, and the golden threads of faith run through all the rest of her web.
28270-hypolympia-or-the-gods-in-the-isla:
Edmund Gosse's Hypolympia, or The Gods in the Island, London, 1901, is an ironic fantasy in play form. On a terrace high above the sea, Aphrodite and Eros arrive in a neglected English country house garden, feeling strange new sensations: breathlessness, weariness, and something like mortality. The sea, woods, and yellow fields look nothing like Cythera, yet strangely like it.

Gosse asks what happens when old gods meet a modern, prosaic world. His dialogue is witty, learned, and gently sad. The fantasy offers a short, elegant meditation on myth, age, and the loss of divine ease.
2858-cressy:
Bret Harte set Cressy in a California schoolhouse in Tuolumne County, where a young schoolmaster of twenty tries to look severe beyond his years. He throws away wildflowers and adopts an air of exhausted experience as he faces his pupils, including Cressy McKinstry. The school building itself, assigned by the county board, frames a story of frontier manners and feeling.

The plot turns on small tokens and misunderstandings, such as a bunch of sprigs bound with a long filament of brown hair that the master recognizes as Cressy's. Harte balances comedy about the teacher's dignity with a tender account of affection across a social gap. The novel shows his later California manner, quieter than his gold-rush sketches but just as observant.
30974-jimbo-a-fantasy:
Algernon Blackwood wrote this fantasy, first published in 1909 and held here in a Macmillan edition of 1930, in the Caravan Library, printed in Great Britain. Its eighteen chapters run from Rabbits and Miss Lake Comes and Goes through The Shock, On the Edge of Unconsciousness, and Into the Empty House. They continue with His Companion in Prison, The Spell of the Empty House, and The Gallery of Ancient Memories.

Later chapters bring The Means of Escape, The Plunge, The First Flight, The Four Winds, Pleasures of Flight, An Adventure, The Call of the Body, Preparation, Off, and Home. The book opens by saying Jimbo's governess surely ought to have known better, but did not. It adds that if she had, then Jimbo would never have met the adventures that came to him. It is a strange, dreamlike fantasy of a child, an empty house, and flight.
3491-missy:
Dana Gatlin writes a novel about Melissa, called Missy, a girl growing up in the town of Roseboro. The chapters follow her from Sunday school and a first strange feeling she calls the flame divine, through romance, blushing, business, and a happy downfall. Missy tackles romance in her own way, influences a boy named Arthur, and cans the cosmos, as one chapter title puts it.

Gatlin writes childhood and youth with humor and warmth, letting Missy learn by mistakes rather than by lectures. The book's small town world feels real, with friends, family, and church shaping each day. Young readers and adults who enjoy old fashioned growing up stories will find a lively heroine at its center.
3494-bluebeard-a-musical-fantasy:
Kate Douglas Wiggin retells the old tale of Bluebeard as a musical fantasy for young performers and audiences. The story follows a rich, bearded husband whose wives vanish, and a curious young wife who opens a forbidden door. Wiggin shapes the grim fairy tale into a play with songs, keeping the fright at a level children can enjoy.

The piece was made for school and home performance, with parts that let young actors sing, act, and play at mystery. Its charm lies in turning a dark legend into a lively entertainment. Families and teachers looking for a classic children's play will find a short, performable version of a famous tale.
35279-the-literature-of-ecstasy:
The Literature of Ecstasy is a work of literary criticism by Albert Mordell. Boni and Liveright published it in New York in 1921. Mordell had earlier written on the erotic motive in literature. He had also written on Dante. The book argues that ecstasy, not rhythm, is the heart of poetry.

Twelve chapters build the case step by step. Early chapters treat the psychology of ecstasy. Later ones claim that prose is the natural language of the ecstatic kind. Blank verse and free verse are treated as forms of prose. The book holds that moral and social ideas become poetry when written with ecstasy. A chapter on love ecstasy in Arabian poetry closes the argument.
38710-istar-of-babylon-a-phantasy:
Istar of Babylon, subtitled A Phantasy, is a historical novel by Margaret Horton Potter, printed in New York and London in 1902. Potter dedicates it to her husband and dear comrade. The tale is a long romance of ancient Babylon, in three books: the journey, the great city, and what follows.

Chapters move from the sea and a vow, into the East, to the gate of God. Inside Babylon, readers find the sanctuary of Istar, a Babylonish household, King Belshazzar, and the feast of Tammuz. Bankers, priests, soldiers, and strange gods crowd the streets. Potter writes rich, learned scenes of the ancient city. The book is a lush specimen of the biblical-age romances once much loved.
4088-sir-walter-scott-and-the-border-min:
Andrew Lang's study of Scott and the Border Minstrelsy traces how Scott gathered, shaped, and sometimes remade the ballads of the Anglo-Scottish border. Sampled verses tell of a host besieging Maitland, of barks laden with spoil, and of England claimed by heritage.

Lang weighs Scott's sources, his edits, and his genius for giving old songs new life. The book suits readers who love ballads and literary history, showing how a nation's songs were saved, and changed, by one great collector. It pairs well with the Minstrelsy itself. Ballad lovers will return to it often.
44791-lady-byron-vindicated-a-history-of:
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Lady Byron Vindicated, a history of the Byron controversy from its beginning in 1816 to the present time, printed at London in 1870. The publishers state their case at once: the subject is of painful notoriety, but their regard for Stowe and her truthfulness places their imprint on the book.

Stowe had published Lady Byron's true story in a magazine, and counter statements poured in. This volume is her reply, defending her narrative and her motives. She had known Lady Byron and believed the poet's widow had suffered a monstrous wrong in her marriage. The quarrel over Byron's sins split literary England, and Stowe, the most famous woman writer alive, chose her side in print.
45843-writings-in-connection-with-the-do:
Marcus Dods edited Writings in Connection with the Donatist Controversy, Volume Three of the Works of Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, in a new English text at Edinburgh in 1872. A note to subscribers from T and T Clark heads the volume. Clark thanks subscribers for a kind take up of the Augustine set. The Anti Pelagian Works, Volume One, came out with this volume.

Clark pledges that no pains will be spared to make the set worthy. The first issue of the second year will hold the Letters and the treatises against Faustus. The Ante Nicene Series is now done, the note says. Clark hopes its readers will move to Augustine. Works of Chrysostom will follow in time. The volume itself holds Augustine's case against the Donatist split in the African church.
47444-the-gastronomic-regenerator-a-simp:
Alexis Soyer, the famous chef of the Reform Club in London, wrote this great cookery book, The Gastronomic Regenerator, in a sixth edition printed at London in 1849. The catalog title is a line about kitchen plans. The book offers a simplified and entirely new system of cookery. It holds nearly two thousand practical receipts suited to the income of all classes.

Plans show how kitchens of every size are to be built and furnished, from a royal palace to a humble cottage. Soyer was the most famous cook in England, a showman who also fed soldiers and the poor. He dedicated the book to the Duke of Cambridge. The work is a monument of Victorian cookery, science and theatre together.
47683-daisy:
Daisy is a short tale for the young by Marshall Saunders, author of Beautiful Joe, published by Charles Banes at Philadelphia. A publisher's note says the story first appeared in England some years before, for a benevolent institution, and is now dressed for a wider public. Its motto is that a little child shall lead them. Four chapters make the whole.

The story opens in a Canadian boarding house. The landlady, a tired and careworn woman, tells the table that a new boarder comes tomorrow: Robertson, a young bank clerk lately from England. The narrator eyes the lad next morning, his eye heavy and his step slow. The little child of the house, willful and neglected by her mother, is to work the change in his warped life.
51456-was-john-bunyan-a-gipsy:
James Simson wrote the pamphlet Was John Bunyan a Gipsy?, issued in 1882 at New York, Edinburgh, and London. Simson had edited a History of the Gipsies in 1865 and written much else on the subject. The pamphlet reworks letters he had sent to the London Daily News and addresses them to students of the universities.

Simson's larger cause runs through the preface. He had worked for years to lift the social proscription on the Romany people in Britain, who had entered the land before 1506 and long lived under bans. He protests that most Britons picture the race as a few wandering tent dwellers, and miss the many who live settled lives. Against that backdrop he argues his startling claim about Bunyan, the tinker preacher who wrote The Pilgrim's Progress.
51887-etiquette-made-easy:
Etiquette Made Easy is a manners manual by Edward Summers Squier. Clode published it in New York, with copyright in 1919. It belongs to a series whose name promises plain instruction. Its contents run from afternoon calls to weddings in short chapters.

At homes, bachelor hosts, and balls open the list of subjects. Cards, dinners, and garden-parties take their turns in the scheme. Introductions, letters, and luncheons occupy the middle of the book. Mourning, musicales, opera, and private theatricals receive their own rules. Smoking, stairs, street etiquette, and table manners close the survey. The first chapter treats the afternoon tea as the model function. It is at once the simplest of social forms, Squier writes. Yet it may expand into a most elaborate affair when required. A visiting card, with a line beneath the name, serves as invitation.
5347-understood-betsy:
Dorothy Canfield's Understood Betsy follows Elizabeth Ann, a timid city girl sent to live with Vermont cousins, where she becomes Betsy. Chapters run from Aunt Harriet's cough and Betsy holding the reins, through a short morning, Betsy going to school. The question of what grade Betsy belongs in leads to a sewing society, new clothes, and a birthday.

Canfield, author of The Bent Twig, writes a classic of children's literature about a child learning to be capable and loved. Illustrated by Ada C. Williamson, the book offers young readers a warm story of farm life, school. The understanding that grows between a girl and her new family.
53799-a-general-view-of-positivism-or-su:
Auguste Comte's summary of his system, in Bridges's translation from the French, appears here in a new edition with an introduction of 1908 by Frederic Harrison. Comte calls it a system of thought and life fitted to the great western republic of the French, Italian, Spanish, British, and German nations. The original bears the date Paris, 1848.

Its mottoes run: reorganisation, without God or king, by the systematic worship of Humanity; man's only right is to do his duty; the intellect should be the servant of the heart. Harrison writes that Positivism is at once a philosophy, a religion, and a scheme of social renewal. He praises Bridges's version of 1865 as accurate, plain, and fully explained.
53802-drowsy:
John Ames Mitchell published Drowsy in nineteen seventeen, a novel that he warns is not a fairy tale. Mitchell had earlier written The Last American and Amos Judd. Angus Macdonall and the author drew the pictures.

Mitchell notes that the wonders of today become the common things of daily life. Wireless sending, he suggests, may be a crude start toward sending by thought itself. Waves of thought, like waves of light, might one day carry a lover's call across space. Space, he writes, is alive with unseen force. The tale builds its marvels on that open, questioning ground.
53811-rescue-the-perishing-personal-work:
Fred Seibert arranged this handbook for new Christians who want to win others to the faith. It came out in 1921 at Winona Lake, Indiana, a famed center of evangelical meetings, and sold for forty cents. Its title takes the words of a well-known hymn.

The book calls itself personal work made easy, with suggestive notes and hints for beginners. Verses stand at the head of its pages: how to answer every man, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Seibert gives the shy believer texts, answers, and a plan for speaking to friends. Readers get a plain tool of the revival age, made for the pocket.
54250-the-albigensian-heresy:
A study of the Albigensian heresy by the Reverend H J Warner. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published it at London in 1922. Cambridge approved the work as a dissertation for a divinity degree. Warner arranges his chapters as source, soil, seed, and system. Rites and ceremonies get a chapter of their own.

His first move challenges a label. The church called the Cathars Manichean, and Warner calls that label a libel. The name carried centuries of sinister association. It justified the severest penalties of church and state. Yet no Manichean writer or emissary left a trace on Cathar teaching. Their dualism differed from the older kind in key points. Warner reconstructs what the southern French heretics actually believed.
55417-the-gentleman-who-vanished-a-psych:
Fergus Hume, the author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, wrote a tale of the unseen world that White of London published in 1890. A verse at the front warns against tampering with that world. Chapter one is named Flying From Justice.

It is a close night at the end of June in London. The heavy air is charged with storm. The crowds sweep through the lit streets, heedless of the sky. In a fine room off Piccadilly, two young men sit at cards. The chapter names promise the path of the tale: a recluse, the dissection of a soul, a curious change, and the tortures of hell. A modern Judas and a rising again close the list.
56142-patsy:
Patsy is a novel by Stacpoole, first published in 1908 and many times reprinted, here issued in a shilling series alongside works by Conrad, Wells, Haggard and Service. The contents promise thirty-seven chapters of Irish hunting, household comedy and ghosts.

The opening chapter, Where the Wild Geese Fly, sets an Irish country scene in high romantic style. A watcher sees a flock pass and fade into the amber distance like a wreath of smoke. To the left stand the hills of Glynn, where the golden eagle has its eyrie. Later titles introduce Patsy, a form in the wood, a hiring, and a battle in the yard, promising a story of servants, gentry and sport.
61716-the-devil-s-motor-a-fantasy:
The Devil's Motor, a fantasy by Marie Corelli, is a short allegorical tale with pictures by Arthur Severn. Hodder and Stoughton published it at London. At dead midnight, at the moment when the past hours slip from the grasp of the hours to come, a sound of giant wheels rushes between earth and heaven. A huge car tears at full speed along the line between darkness and dawn.

Its driver stands within, clothed in black and crowned with fire. Bat like wings of woven smoke and flame flare out on either side of him. His face is white as bleached bone, his eyes glow like embers, and a frozen smile, crueller than hate, sits on his lips. On, he cries, without pause, pity, love, or regret. Corelli turns the new motor car into a vision of the devil gathering speed mad mankind.
65912-swat-the-fly-a-one-act-fantasy:
Swat the Fly is a one-act fantasy play by Eleanor Gates. It was copyrighted as a stage work in 1914. The Arrow house in New York issued the book in 1915. Gates also wrote The Poor Little Rich Girl. The cast list mixes people with beasts and one insect. A doctor and a woman inspector head the human side. A boy, a dog, a cat, and a horse follow.

The scene is a garden behind an animal laboratory. A monkey's house and a dog's kennel stand in the garden. The rabbit's hutch rests by the rear wall. The fly itself is a speaking part. Health plays of the day taught clean habits by fancy. The fly stood for dirt and disease in that teaching. Gates lets the beasts plead their case in court-like fun. The play could be read aloud without leave.
6629-mr-midshipman-easy:
Frederick Marryat opens with Nicodemus Easy, a Hampshire gentleman in easy circumstances, married ten years with no child. Most couples find it easy to have a family, Marryat jokes. Keeping one is not always so easy. Easy, wanting what he cannot get, turns philosopher. That is the best trade for a man fit for nothing else. The joke sets a light, teasing tone.

From that start, young Jack Easy goes to sea, where his father's easy notions of equal rights meet the hard discipline of a ship. Marryat, himself a sailor, writes with humor and first-hand knowledge of naval life. Mr. Midshipman Easy is a classic comic sea tale, full of fun, folly, and growing sense.
6676-rosy:
Mrs. Molesworth, author of Carrots and Cuckoo Clock, tells of Rosy, Colin, and Felix, with pictures by Walter Crane. Rosy meets Beata, sheds tears, thinks things over, and faces a strike in the schoolroom, a present from Mr. Furniture, and a hole in the floor. A parcel and a fright, stings for Bee, and good out of evil follow in turn.

Molesworth writes for young readers with warmth and a keen sense of a child's view of grown-up puzzles. Her Rosy is bright, kind, and prone to small scrapes. Rosy is a charming Victorian children's book, full of home, school, and the small dramas that feel large to a child.
67820-arthur-machen-weaver-of-fantasy:
William Francis Gekle wrote Arthur Machen, Weaver of Fantasy, in 1949. The Round Table Press at Millbrook, New York, put it out. Gekle gives the book to Verne on a bare dedication page. His opening quotes a talker on Machen's thirty years of neglect. That neglect, says the quote, is a crime for the house-top.

The speaker was James Branch Cabell, writing back in 1918, Gekle notes. The thirty years of neglect have almost doubled since then, he adds. Indeed Machen has suffered a lifetime of neglect, in his verdict. The loss has been the world's, which so blindly accorded it. Machen's uncanny genius deserved better of readers and collectors, he holds. Voices of librarians and collectors rise in protest through the study. Gekle gives a life, a bibliography, and a plea for the fantasist.
68539-the-shakespeare-garden-club-a-fant:
Mabel Moran wrote the Shakespeare Garden Club, a fantasy, in 1919. Moran sat in a Larchmont garden club. A room in a cottage at Stratford opens the one-act piece. Chairs stand in a semi-circle there. A long chest serves as desk for the presiding officer.

Ann Hathaway receives two merry wives at her door first. They are welcome guests, not members. A meeting of the club is to be grave and solemn today. The president of the club is Lady Macbeth herself in it. Portia is its attorney-at-law among the officers named. Jessica, Shylock's daughter, is treasurer of the club there. No one dares cross those officers, the talk jokes lightly. Perdita, Cordelia, Desdemona, and Juliet stand in the cast list. Moran gives Shakespeare's women a club meeting of their own.
69334-high-class-cookery-made-easy:
Hart wrote a cook book for young ladies and new cooks. She had run a hands-on cooking class in several towns and had tested her recipes there. The book was printed in Edinburgh by Lorimer and Gillies. Its aim was to suit homes that must watch their costs, unlike many cook books of its day.

Early pages stress clean pans and good stock, since sauces rest on both. Then come soups, fish, made dishes, and main courses, with sauces for each. Later parts cover joints of meat, puddings, vegetables, cakes, and pastry. Clear steps let a new cook follow along and build skill meal by meal, from first stock to last cake.
69601-the-escape-of-alice-a-christmas-fa:
Vincent Starrett wrote The Escape of Alice, a short Christmas fantasy printed in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 1919. The booklet was made in private for Luther and Elinore Brewer, who sent it to friends as a holiday gift. Starrett was a Chicago writer and book lover.

Alice slips out of a picture in her famous book and climbs down a bookshop shelf. She eats a few crumbs of cake and grows at once to a schoolgirl of thirteen. Then she picks her own book off the shelf and offers to buy it. The old bookseller, lost in thought, takes her money as if nothing were odd. The tale plays gently with a classic every reader knows.
69842-gle-and-the-elf-a-fantasy:
Toland's verse fantasy, issued by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1887, is printed with photogravures after drawings by artists including Church, Mowbray, and Gibson. The narrator rests his oars on a stream at moonrise, where nymphs are at play beneath the willows. A fair vision rises on the tide: Ægle, a daughter of water, laden with lilies to hide her blushes.

A young woodland elf, perched on a tree-top with a quizzical face, surprises her as she admires herself. She sinks at once amid ripples of light, waving her form from his sight. Three more naiads rise, swimming and trimming a cedar branch aside, while the elf plunges blindly into the tide after the vanished company.
71312-leprosy:
Leprosy, In Its Clinical and Pathological Aspects is a medical work by Dr G Armauer Hansen, inspector-general of leprosy in Norway, and Dr Carl Looft, formerly of the Lungegaards Hospital. It was printed at Bristol in 1895 in Norman Walker's translation. Photographs and coloured plates illustrate the disease's forms.

The authors' preface says their earlier Norwegian work was unknown to many investigators, whose statements they found premature and ill founded. Hansen had dealt with the disease for more than twenty years, and his name is bound to its study as the finder of its bacillus. The translator calls his knowledge second to none. The book sums up the Norwegian school's findings for English readers at a time when leprosy science was sharply disputed.
74629-the-musgrave-controversy:
The Musgrave Controversy is a London pamphlet of papers on the late peace, priced at one shilling. At its head stand the Devonshire instructions, voted at the Castle of Exon on October 5, 1769. The freeholders of Devon order their two members of Parliament to press an enquiry. A Crown magistrate had refused to examine evidence laid before him.

The papers say that secrets touching the safety of the kingdom were likely lost by that refusal. Men accused of dishonoring the government went unpunished and uncensured. The freeholders also demand shorter Parliaments. An address by Musgrave, a physician at Plymouth, opens the case for the county meeting at Exeter.
76716-the-palace-of-fantasy:
The Palace of Fantasy, or The Bard's Imagery, with Other Poems, is a verse volume by Hardy, printed at London by Smith, Elder and Company in 1845. Hardy had already published Hours of Thought, or Poetic Musings. The advertisement thanks the periodical press for its favourable notice of that former book. The hope of the new one, Hardy says, is to lead readers to look through Nature up to Nature's God.

The preface explains the poem's machinery. The work may be divided into the descriptive, the allegorical and the imaginative. In the Saloon of Imagery they admire the pictured tapestry. Then Dan Fantasy deputes his favourite companion, the Bard, to guide them through his wide domain. They survey the hidden things of earth: marvels of nature, art, literature and science. The moral is to forego grovelling for loftier pursuits.
77301-ossianic-controversy:
John MacPherson, a Gaelic parish minister, gave the lecture printed as Ossianic Controversy to the Greenock Highland Society, and it was issued at Greenock in 1873. MacPherson opens with the origin of the doubt that hung over the Ossian poems and the grounds that first woke suspicion among men of letters. He goes back to the middle of the last century, to John Home of the tragedy Douglas and his talk of Gaelic poetry.

Home had read a piece by Jerome Stone in the Scots Magazine and put its claims to Professor Ferguson at Edinburgh, who backed them. James Macpherson, then a tutor in 1759, held pieces of old Gaelic verse and showed one to Home. The lecture weighs that whole chain of proof.
77752-bibliography-of-the-bacon-shakespe:
Bibliography of the Bacon-Shakespeare Controversy, with notes and extracts, by W H Wyman, was published by Peter G Thomson of Cincinnati in 1884. The question of the book is who wrote the plays of Shakespeare. A comic line from an old play stands as its motto, crying Shikspur, Shikspur, who wrote it. The volume lists every book, pamphlet, and article on the fight that Wyman could find.

In July 1882 Wyman had issued a small private list of sixty three titles. Matter piled up so fast that he made this fuller book, the work of his leisure evenings. He holds no doubt himself that Shakespeare wrote the plays. Still, he prints the adverse theories and the answers side by side, so any reader can judge. The fight, he grants, has one good fruit: it drives men to study the plays.
77817-escape-and-fantasy:
George Rostrevor wrote Escape and Fantasy, a book of poems printed in New York in 1919. The title states the plan: to flee the day's dull work into dream and fancy. The first poem, The Change, sets a clerk among cash and ledger books by day.

By twilight the same man ranges over fay birds and phantom flowers, and sings mad songs in the evening. Poems on Orpheus, the river, spring rain in London, and the lotus eaters follow. A sea-maid, a grey bird, and a haunted street keep the mood of longing. The book is a young poet's bid for beauty in the year after the Great War.
78189-the-virgin-and-the-gipsy:
D H Lawrence wrote the short novel The Virgin and the Gipsy, and it came out in London in 1930, after his death. A note in the book says it lacks his final revision and was printed from the manuscript just as it stood. The tale is set in a bleak stone village in the north, near old cotton mills.

The story opens with a scandal from years before, when a vicar's wife left her husband and ran off with a young man who had no money. Her two small girls grow up in the rectory under their father, grandmother, and aunt. Lawrence traces the stiff, pious life of that house and the strain it lays on the girls. The work is read for its sharp eye, its feel for place, and its clash between strict duty and free desire.
78605-tales-of-the-uneasy:
Tales of the Uneasy, published in London in 1911, gathers nine stories by Violet Hunt, among them The Telegram, The Operation, The Prayer, The Coach, and The Tiger-Skin. The first tale opens on Alice Damer, thirty-five, newly orphaned and seventy thousand pounds richer, with a fine house in Lower Seymour Street and every social door still open. Nothing has changed for her except that her mother is dead, and she must now take a paid companion to keep her place in the world.

Hunt draws her heroine with a cool, exact eye: pretty still, a quiet flirt, already tired of dancing and content to sit out. The unease of the title grows from such small shifts, fortunes and feelings slightly out of joint. These are polished stories of manners with a shadow across them, by a novelist who knew the society she wrote about from inside.
78785-i-thought-of-daisy:
I Thought of Daisy is a tale by Edmund Wilson, out at New York in nineteen twenty-nine. The tale opens past a low red brick house in the town, with a white door, a brass knob, and brass name plates. New green and white shades and green bloom boxes mark it as a smart spot of those days. The tell man rings with a friend, and a click lock sings past the door.

They were friends of a named host, men and maids said to hold gifts or charm. The stairs were soft laid in green. The tall host in feast dress met them at the door with a smile. Bright rooms held pale green drink cups, a bruised fruit cloth past a couch, and framed draws for the dress of a dance play. Maids in bright paint and cloth stood past the walls like those draws.
and-thus-he-came-a-christmas-fantasy: Cyrus Townsend Brady writes a Christmas fantasy called And Thus He Came, in sections on the baby, the child, the friend, and the workman. The tale imagines Christ coming again into the modern world, meeting its people in humble guise. Brady's gentle fantasy suits the season, joining wonder to a call for kindness.
bluebeard-a-musical-fantasy:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote Bluebeard as a musical fantasy, a satire dedicated to conductor Walter Damrosch, the friend whose art form she treats irreverently. Her preface mocks the lecture-recitals that taught American audiences to fear Wagner. Learned critics, she says, explained every motive in the Ring. Wiggin answers with a mock-serious guide to an imaginary Wagner opera on Bluebeard.

Her cast lists Bluebeard as a wealthy baritone of dubious morals and Fatima as his seventh wife. Sister Anne, a mercenary mother, and rescuing brother Mustapha complete the family. A chorus of headless wives sings from the sidelines. The lecture analyzes motives for Fatima, the key, and Bluebeard himself with straight-faced nonsense. Readers get a playful spoof of opera scholarship, fairy tale, and Wagner worship in one short book.
britannica-1911-acatalepsy: Acatalepsy is a term from ancient scepticism, the school of philosophy that doubted whether knowledge is possible at all. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it in one line as incomprehensibility, the state of a thing that cannot be grasped or understood. The word joins a Greek privative prefix, meaning not, to a verb meaning to seize. For sceptics, naming that limit mattered: if things cannot be seized by the mind, certain knowledge cannot be claimed.
britannica-1911-autopsy: Autopsy means personal examination, from Greek words for self and sight. Its specific sense is post-mortem examination. A dead body is examined after death. The purpose is ascertaining the cause of death. Necropsy is a synonym sometimes used. That word derives from the Greek for corpse. The entry is brief and definitional only. It points readers to Coroner for legal procedure and to Medical Jurisprudence for the examination's role in law.
britannica-1911-bangorian-controversy:
The Bangorian controversy was a church dispute of the early 1700s in England. It opened in 1716 with the posthumous printing of George Hickes's Constitution of the Christian Church, in which that non-juring bishop cast out all but his own party. Benjamin Hoadly, newly made bishop of Bangor, answered fast and ably.

Hoadly's book backed the state's sway in church matters and proposed sincerity as the only test of truth. His sermon of 31 March 1717, preached before George I on the nature of Christ's kingdom, went further. The 1911 Britannica entry quotes its thrust: no visible church on earth holds Christ's delegated rule, and tests of orthodoxy are worth little. A committee of Convocation reported against him that May.
britannica-1911-cherkasy:
Cherkasy is a town of Russia in the government of Kiev, set 96 miles south-east of Kiev on the right bank of the Dnieper. Its people numbered 15,740 in 1883 and 26,619 in 1897. The entry calls its people Little Russians, most of them working in farming and gardening. Sugar and tobacco making and spirit distilling give the town its industry.

Cherkasy was an important town of the Ukraine in the 15th century, the entry notes. It stayed so under Polish rule until the revolt of the Cossack hetman Chmielnicki in 1648. Russia annexed the town in 1795. The short entry thus links a river port and farm town to its Polish, Cossack and Russian past in a few lines.
britannica-1911-daisy:
Daisy, from an old English phrase meaning day's eye, is the name of the plants of the genus Bellis, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives them a nature entry. The genus holds ten species, found in Europe and the Mediterranean lands. The common daisy is the only one of the genus in the British Isles.

The common daisy is a perennial, plentiful in pastures and on banks across Europe and in Asia Minor, and brought in as a foreign plant in North America. Its stem is short, and its leaves form a rosette close to the ground. The flowers run from March to November, and at times in winter. Each head stands alone, with pink or white outer florets and a yellow disk. Garden forms are many, with coloured flowers that make fine borders for walks. One odd form bears a brood of small heads round the main one.
britannica-1911-embassy:
Embassy is the office of an ambassador, or, more broadly, the mission on which an ambassador of one power is sent to another. The word also covers the body of officials attached to such a mission, whether short-lived or lasting. It also names the official home of an ambassador.

The entry is short and turns last to the word's own history. “Embassy” was first “ambassy,” the form used in the 17th century but judged quite out of date by Johnson's time. “Ambassy” comes from the Old French ambassée. That form came through Portuguese and Italian words from a lost medieval Latin ambactiata, from ambactiare, to go on a mission. For the substance behind the word, readers are sent on to the entries on the ambassador, on exterritoriality, and on diplomacy, where the working rules of such missions are treated.
britannica-1911-epilepsy:
Epilepsy, from Greek words for “upon” and “to seize,” or Falling Sickness, is a term for a nervous disorder marked by a fit of sudden loss of consciousness with convulsions. The long medical entry warns that far slighter shows of the disease may be just as telling. Epilepsy was well known in ancient times and was seen as a special stroke of the gods.

Hence its old names: morbus sacer and morbus divus, the sacred and divine sickness, and morbus comitialis, since an assembly broke up when a member was seized. The entry sets out three marked kinds of seizure, le grand mal, le petit mal, and Jacksonian epilepsy. The entry follows the course of the great fit, then turns to treatment. Surgery, it says, is still in its infancy, save for Jacksonian cases, where removing a tumour or raising a depressed fracture often ends the seizures.
britannica-1911-hypocrisy:
Hypocrisy is pretence, or the false assumption of a high character, above all in matters of religious belief or practice, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a very short entry. The piece is a word study. 

The Greek word from which hypocrisy derives, through old French, meant in the first place the acting of a part on the stage. Its root verb meant to give an answer, to speak dialogue, and to play a part on the stage. From that stage sense came the later meaning, to practise dissimulation, to seem what one is not.
britannica-1911-jassy:
Jassy, the capital of its department in Rumania, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the river Bahlui, west of the Pruth and the Russian frontier, with 78,067 people in 1900. Rail lines link it with Galatz on the Danube, with Kishinev and with Czernowitz.

The country round Jassy is one of uplands and woods, with monasteries and mineral springs near by. The town itself stands amid vineyards and gardens, partly on two hills and partly in the hollow between them. Its old houses of timber and plaster were mostly swept away after 1860, when brick and stone came into general use. Good streets were then cut through the network of narrow lanes. Jassy is the seat of the metropolitan of Moldavia and of a Roman Catholic archbishop, and churches and synagogues abound.
britannica-1911-leprosy:
Leprosy fills a long medical account in the 1911 Britannica. The disease is traced to the Nile lands by 1500 B.C. It ruled as the great sickness of the medieval Christian world. In the writers' own day it stayed common in Asia, Africa, South America, and the West Indies. Patches of it held on in parts of Europe.

Cause is laid to a germ found by Armauer Hansen in 1871. The germ breeds masses of new cells in the flesh. Skin and deeper parts thicken, waste, and lose their form. Old art, such as a Holbein picture of 1516, shows the knobs and blotches well. Later pages sort true leprosy from diseases once mixed with it. Homes for the sick in Norway and elsewhere close the survey.
britannica-1911-marprelate-controversy:
The Marprelate controversy was a war of pamphlets fought in fifteen eighty eight and fifteen eighty nine. On one side stood a Puritan writer who used the false name Martin Marprelate. On the other stood defenders of the Established Church of England. Martin's tracts use harsh and personal abuse of church leaders. They claim that the writer has many strong backers behind him.

While Martin held Puritan doctrine as a whole, his chief target was the bishops. His pamphlets came from a secret press set up by John Penry, a Welsh Puritan. The printer Robert Waldegrave helped run that press from midsummer fifteen eighty eight. The first tract, called the Epistle, came out at Molesey in November. It answers a defence of the church written by Dean John Bridges. A bishop's reply was too long and dull to match it.
britannica-1911-pansy:
Pansy, also called heartsease, is a garden flower covered in a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The flower has been grown so long that its wild source is in doubt. As seen in gardens it is a made form, unlike any wild plant. Most hold it to be a bred form of Viola tricolor, a cornfield weed.

Tests with seed from the wild plant back that view, since they yield pansy like blooms. Long choice breeding made the blooms larger and more round. It also spread and deepened their colours in new ways. The entry sorts show types by ground colour, such as white grounds and yellow grounds. Fancy types from Belgium bear blotched and streaked petals. Bedding violas, bred from hardier kin, are praised for mass colour in spring and summer beds.
britannica-1911-pleurisy:
Pleurisy, a swelling of the skin that lines the chest, is set out in a health entry in the 1911 Britannica. Small germs that invade that skin cause the ill, the text says at the start. Spread from a sick lung or near part can bring it on as well. Three steps mark the change in the sick skin as it grows worse. First comes a rush of blood and soak of the skin.

Next a coat of lymph spreads on the chest skin in thin or thick sheets. Bands of that coat can glue the two skins as one in time. Last comes a flow of fluid into the chest space in bad cases. Dry forms stop at the lymph step with no fluid at all. Great flows can crush a lung to a scrap of its size.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostasy:
Apostasy, from Greek words for standing away, means in its root sense desertion of a post or giving up a state of life. A person who freely takes up a definite state cannot leave it without becoming an apostate, the article argues. Most authors, following Benedict XIV, distinguish three kinds. Apostasy from faith comes when a Christian gives up belief. Apostasy from order comes when a cleric abandons the clerical state. Apostasy from religion comes when a religious leaves religious life.

A gloss on Gregory IX's decretals adds two more kinds, disobedience to lawful command and repetition of baptism, since repeat baptizers seem to desert their first baptism. The article judges the first no specific offence, since all sin involves disobedience, and the second more a matter of heresy and irregularity than apostasy. Readers get a careful sorting of a word often used loosely, with canon law distinctions kept plain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archpriest-co:
The Archpriest Controversy arose in England when the Holy See appointed George Blackwell archpriest, with authority over England's and Scotland's secular clergy, on 7 March of 1598. The last member of the old hierarchy, Goldwell, bishop of St. Asaph's, died in 1585, and Cardinal Allen then exercised informal jurisdiction with papal acquiescence and common consent of some three hundred missionary priests. After Allen's death in 1594 the lack of a superior was keenly felt.

Trouble at the English College in Rome had already set Jesuits and secular clergy at odds, sharpened by dissensions among priests jailed at Wisbech. In 1597 Father Persons, who ran the Jesuit mission in England, travelled to Rome and settled college troubles by becoming rector himself. Some secular clergy, resenting growing Jesuit influence, resisted Blackwell's appointment, and the entry follows a quarrel over who should govern a persecuted church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-easter-contro:
The Easter controversy ran through three distinct phases in church history, and this entry states each with care. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with the first phase, under Pope Victor about the year 190. The dioceses of Asia kept an older tradition. Their rule: the moon's fourteenth day, when Jews sacrificed the lamb, must always mark the life-giving pasch feast, ending the fast that day whatever the weekday.

Later phases turned on other points of the Easter reckoning, and the entry follows them through councils and scholars to the settlement of the date. It cites Duchesne, Kellner, and the English Historical Review among its guides. For readers of the calendar, it untangles a dispute that once split East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecstasy:
Supernatural ecstasy is a state holding two elements while it lasts, one inward and unseen, one bodily and visible. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the inward half: the mind fastens on a religious subject while the senses fall quiet, shutting out outer sensation. Considerable trouble follows in waking such sensation, whether the ecstatic wills it or others try to quicken the organs.

Hagiology attests ecstasies granted to many saints, and even today's free-thinkers hesitate to deny facts on so solid a base. They no longer try, as their eighteenth-century forebears did, to explain them away as fraud. Instead they seek natural causes at any cost, since their principles deny the supernatural, a move the entry notes with dry logic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heresy:
Heresy, in the thirteen-section article read here, begins with connotation and definition. From the Greek airesis, a choice, it was applied by Josephus to the Sadducees, Pharisees, and Essenes and by Paul's accusers to the Nazarenes. Aquinas defines it as a species of infidelity in those who, having professed Christ's faith, corrupt its dogmas, accepting only such parts of the deposit of faith as commend themselves to them. There the believer accepts the whole as proposed by the Church.

The article distinguishes heresy from apostasy, which abandons the faith wholly, and from schism, which separates from church unity, noting that not all schismatics are heretics. It grades heresy by degrees, requires pertinacity for formal, willed heresy over material error, and traces motives from intellectual pride to political interest. Later sections cover its gravity, origins, patristic teaching, church legislation, jurisdiction over heretics, reception of converts, and role in history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-paulinus:
Hugh Paulinus Serenus Cressy was an English Benedictine monk and doctor of theology, born at Thorpe-Salvin in Yorkshire about 1605 and dead at East Grinstead in 1674. Son of Hugh Cressy and Margery d'Oylie, he was schooled at Wakefield, entered Oxford at fourteen, and took degrees in 1623 and 1627. Merton College made him a fellow, and he took orders in the Established Church.

Cressy served as chaplain to Lord Wentworth and then to Lord Falkland, following him to Ireland in 1638 and becoming dean of Leighlin. After Falkland's death at Newbury in 1643, he travelled with Charles Berkeley through Catholic Europe, converted at Rome in 1646, and went on to Paris for further instruction. The entry follows a scholar whose path ran from Oxford fellow to Catholic monk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hypocrisy:
Hypocrisy, from Greek words meaning to answer on the stage, means playing a part, feigning or pretending. More narrowly, it is the pretension to qualities one does not possess, or putting on a false show of virtue or religion. Its malice matches lying's malice: in both, mind and outward show disagree.

For morality it matters little whether the gap appears in words, as in formal lies, or in demeanour, as in simulation. Mere concealment of one's own sin, unless legitimate authority interrogates, does not straightaway count as hypocrisy. To measure its sinfulness, Aquinas separates its two elements, want of goodness and pretence of having it. Intending both is plainly grievous sin, since it joins lacking goodness with claiming it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jassy:
Jassy, now Iasi in Romania, is covered here as both a city and a Latin diocese. The town stands on a fertile plain beside the River Bahluiu, a branch of the Pruth, and counted about eighty thousand people when the entry was written. Its church of the Three Saints and monastery of the Three Hierarchs rank among its chief monuments.

Moldavia's capital from the sixteenth century until its union with Wallachia in 1859, Jassy was often held by Russian, Polish, or Austrian forces. It hosted Greek and Russian church talks in 1642 and a Russo-Turkish treaty in 1792. The Latin diocese, refounded in 1884 after a long line of earlier sees and prefects, then served about ninety thousand Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jealousy:
Jealousy, treated here as the same fault as envy, gets a careful moral definition in this Catholic Encyclopedia entry. It is sorrow at another person's good fortune, felt because that success seems to lessen one's own worth. Its core wrong lies in opposing charity, the love that should make us rejoice at a neighbour's good.

Such envy usually counts as a grave sin, though small matter or lack of thought can make it light. It turns worst when aimed at another's spiritual good, and it breeds hatred, backbiting, and glee at others' misfortune. Yet not every pang at a rival's rise is jealousy: grief rooted in a just sense that the gain was undeserved, or fear it will do harm, can be sound.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leprosy:
Leprosy proper, lepra tuberculosa, is a chronic infectious disease from the bacillus leprae. It forms growths in skin, mucous membranes, nerves, bones, and inner organs, bringing deformity and usually death. It differs from other skin troubles also called lepra, such as psoriasis. The disease was not uncommon in India by the fifteenth century B.C. and in Japan by the tenth. Egypt has always been seen as its route to the West, in the Ebers Papyrus of the sixteenth century B.C.

 Manetho's romance that Egypt cast out a mass of Hebrew lepers aside, the Exodus people were touched by it. Phoenician sailors carried it to Syria and trading lands, hence Hippocrates' Phoenician disease.  The Jews' dispersion after the Restoration and Roman armies' campaigns spread it through Western Europe, infecting colonies in Spain, Gaul, and Britain. In Christian times councils, popes, kings' laws, and leper-houses shaped its treatment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-luss:
Melchior Lussy, a Swiss statesman born at Stans in Unterwalden in 1529, died there in 1606. Even young he held offices, fought in the campaigns of 1557 and 1573, and served ten times as high bailiff of his canton. He often acted as envoy of the Confederacy in France, Spain, and elsewhere. With Abbot Joachim Eichhorn of Einsiedeln, he spoke for the Catholic cantons at the Council of Trent.

He reached Trent on 16 March 1562 and stayed until June 1563, swearing in the Catholic confederates' name to adopt and uphold the council's decrees. From then on he laboured tirelessly to plant those decrees in Switzerland, taking charge of them firmly in 1564 and never letting them slip. A friend of St. Charles Borromeo, he arranged a papal nunciature to Switzerland and backed Nuncio Borromeo of Vercelli on his arrival in 1579, and every later nuncio too. In 1583 he pilgrimaged to Jerusalem.
cressy:
Bret Harte opens this novel at the Indian Spring school in Tuolumne County, California, where the young master, John Ford, unlocks a schoolhouse that was once a church. Ford is twenty, severe beyond his years, and proud of an air of exhausted experience. His scholars include the girl of the title, Cressy McKinstry, the brightest and most troublesome presence in the room.

Harte builds the story on the schoolmaster's slow undoing. Cressy's family, her admirers, and the rough politics of the settlement draw Ford out of his professional shell. The romance that grows between master and pupil runs against her father's world of feuds and pistols. It is one of Harte's fullest California novels, with the schoolroom as its stage and its comic scenes built from lessons gone wrong.
daisy:
A novel by Susan Warner, under her pen name Elizabeth Wetherell, fills this 1868 book in the Ward, Lock edition. Warner had won fame with The Wide, Wide World and Queechy. Daisy, the heroine, tells her own life in the first person.

She says her bright years lasted till her eleventh summer, when faith entered her days. Contents name Miss Pinshon, the multiplication table, school, shopping, and French dresses. South and North and Entered for the War mark the turn toward the Civil War in the later chapters. Dressing rooms, schools, and army talk fill the middle. The book joins a girl's growth to strict Christian teaching, in the manner that made Warner a household name.
doe-osti-3399504-autonomous-radiation-ca:
Matthew Aaron Cohn's Autonomous Radiation Cartographer System Training Manual, Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26912 issued August 3, 2026, teaches end users to run a radiation-mapping robot. The ARC is a fully autonomous radiation detection system. It is built on the Spot robot platform made by Boston Dynamics. That four-legged machine walks the robot through the spaces to be surveyed.

The manual's chapters run from vocabulary and key terms through the Spot platform itself. Safety and security protocols, operating procedures, a user interface guide, and maintenance follow. Its learning objectives promise that a trained user can state the system's capabilities and limits. The user can operate it in manual and autonomous modes. The user can perform routine maintenance and basic troubleshooting, and respond correctly to emergencies. The training exists so survey work in radiation areas can be done by a machine instead of a person carrying a detector.
entertaining-made-easy:
Emily Rose Burt takes the work out of parties in Entertaining Made Easy, a 1919 volume in the Made Easy Series. Her opening claim is plain: it is fun to entertain if you do not make hard work of it. Plans sort by occasion: socials and parties, outdoor affairs, birthdays, showers, and weddings of every season.

A Smiles Social, an Aviation Meet, and a Mock Canteen fill the first section. Children get a Pussy Cat Party with pen-and-ink ears and games of Poor Pussy and Kitty Kitty. Wedding schemes run from a Wild Rose summer wedding to a Colonial winter one. Much material came by permission from Woman's Home Companion and The Ladies' Home Journal.
hearts-of-controversy:
Alice Meynell gathered six literary essays in Hearts of Controversy, printed by Burns and Oates in 1918. Some Thoughts of a Reader of Tennyson opens the book, noting that Tennyson was saluted as great fifty years after his birth and newly detracted from at his centenary. Meynell distinguishes the law of change from the flickering custom of reaction.

Essays follow on Dickens as a man of letters, Swinburne's lyrical poetry and his changed estimates of art, Charlotte and Emily Bronte, and Shakespeare's Charmian, closing with The Century of Moderation. Meynell judges reputations as a poet-critic, interested in how taste moves. The volume is a small masterclass in early twentieth-century literary manners.
little-prudy-s-sister-susy:
Sophie May tells here of Susy, oldest of the Parlin girls. Hurst and Company published the book in New York. She dedicates it to her little niece Katie Clarke. Prudy still forces her way into her sister's story, May admits.

The preface hopes readers learn from Prudy's slow winter of pain. Trouble, sent in love, should make children gentle and patient. Contents promise secrets, Christmas, wings, and moral courage. Susy's birthday and a farewell close the family tale. Katie Clarke receives the book with her auntie's love. Rosy Frances, Eastman, and Mary appear among Susy's chapters.
missy:
Dana Gatlin's novel follows Melissa M., called Missy, who has just turned ten. Chapter one finds her home from Sunday school with a brand-new feeling. She looks back on her seven-year-old self as a stranger: a silly who still believed in Santa Claus. Now, she feels, she is almost grown up.

The contents promise Missy tackling romance, influencing Arthur, and blushing through several chapters. One chapter is titled Missy Cans the Cosmos. Gatlin writes the comedy of a child who overestimates her new wisdom. The book belongs to the era's popular fiction about lively Southern girls growing up.
mr-midshipman-easy:
Frederick Marryat's sea novel opens in Hampshire with Mr. Nicodemus Easy. Easy is a rich married man who longs for children. After ten childless years he turns to philosophy. He settles on grand talk of rights, equality, and shares of the earth.

His son Jack later takes those ideas to sea as a midshipman. V1 notes say Jack joins sure all men are equal. Ship life soon teaches him rank, duty, and danger. Marryat had served at sea himself and fills scenes with true detail. The result is a funny, lively tale of a boy growing into an officer.
podcast-joerogan-4OKNS5j0lSY:
Mathematician and writer Eric Weinstein returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2503, a late entry in one of the show's longest guest runs. Weinstein is known for bold claims about physics, universities, and public debate. Rogan mostly sets a topic loose and lets him run.

The talk ranges across science politics, media habits, and Weinstein's long fight to get his own physics ideas a fair hearing. He criticizes the gatekeepers he blames for stale thinking, and Rogan tests the claims as a fan and a skeptic at once. Fans of Weinstein's past visits will find his core themes pressed further here.
podcast-joerogan-nAk8MagnDsY:
Randall Carlson and Graham Hancock appear together in this Joe Rogan Experience segment on lost technology and the Great Pyramids of Egypt. Carlson studies ancient floods and earth changes, while Hancock argues a skilled lost culture came before known history. Together they make the case that the pyramids hide a deeper past.

The two walk through the size, precision, and alignment of the pyramid stones. They ask how ancient builders cut and moved such blocks without modern machines. Rogan presses them on proof and on why experts reject their claims. The talk gives fringe ancient history its fullest hearing.
rosy: Mrs. Molesworth wrote Rosy, with pictures by Walter Crane, and the title page also names her earlier books Carrots, Cuckoo Clock, and Tell Me a Story. The contents list twelve chapters, opening with Rosy, Colin, and Felix, then Beata, Tears, and Ups and Downs. Later chapters include Rosy Thinks Things Over, A Strike in the Schoolroom, Mr. Furniture's Present, The Hole in the Floor, A Parcel and a Fright, and Good Out of Evil. Two pictures are listed, one captioned Manchon.
sir-walter-scott-and-the-border-minstrel:
Andrew Lang published this defense of Sir Walter Scott with Longmans in London in 1910. A preface states the charge plainly: Scott stood suspected of helping to forge the ballad Auld Maitland and passing it off as a true antique. If Scott knew the ballad was a modern fake, Lang writes, then Scott lied on purpose.

Lang answers that Scott took the whole ballad from James Hogg, who had it from oral recitation, as Scott himself firmly held. Letters from Ritson and Hogg and the song's own manuscript back the case. Ballad lovers get a sharp study of honor and evidence.
the-arian-controversy: Title and contents pages present H. M. Gwatkin's The Arian Controversy, a volume in the Epochs of Church History series edited by Mandell Creighton, late Bishop of London. Gwatkin is named as Dixie Professor of Ecclesiastical History at Cambridge. Longmans, Green and Company printed this sixth impression in 1908 for London, New York, Bombay, and Calcutta. Chapters begin with the beginnings of Arianism on page 1, take the Council of Nicaea on page 16, the Eusebian reaction on page 41, and the Council of Sardica on page 61.
the-devil-s-motor-a-fantasy:
Marie Corelli calls The Devil's Motor a fantasy, dated 1910, printed by Hodder and Stoughton with illustrations by Arthur Severn. At dead midnight comes the moment when the hours that are past slip from the grasp of the hours yet to be. A sound of giant wheels comes rushing between earth and heaven.

A huge car tears along the pale line dividing darkness from dawn. Its driver stands clothed in black and crowned with fire, bat-like wings of smoke and flame flaring at his sides, his face white as bleached bone and his eyes glowing like embers. He cries on, without pause, pity, love, or regret, calling all forces bent on man's ruin to follow. Forests drop like broken reeds, seas dry to black mud, and giant cities of smoking chimneys rise as phantom forms ride behind the car.
the-essays-of-arthur-schopenhauer-the-ar:
Arthur Schopenhauer's The Art of Controversy, in T. Bailey Saunders's rendering, teaches how debates are won, fairly or not. Its heads name logic and dialectic, the basis of all dialectic, and then stratagems: the tricks men use to seem right when they are not. Companion pieces take up interest and beauty in art, notes on the mind, and the wisdom of life in aphorisms.

Saunders drew the set from Schopenhauer's posthumous papers, first issued by Julius Frauenstädt and later fleshed out by Eduard Grisebach. The stratagem list still arms debaters and warns the unwary.
the-ghost-a-modern-fantasy: Arnold Bennett wrote The Ghost as a modern fantasy, printed at Boston in 1911 under rights of 1907 and 1911. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapter heads name a splendid cousin, a night at the opera, the cry of Alresca, Rosa's summons, a dagger, a vigil by a bier, a message, a train, and a steamer. Bennett's past books named here include The Old Wives' Tales and Clayhanger. No chapter text is included in this portion.
the-story-of-patsy:
Kate Douglas Wiggin tells here of Patsy. She also wrote The Birds' Christmas Carol. She dedicates the book in remembrance of gladness given to sorrowful little lives. Verses by Mrs. Browning preface it. They tell of young children weeping in the country of the free. Her author's note, dated from New York in March 1889, explains the story's unusual origin.

The original Story of Patsy came first, Wiggin writes. She wrote and sold it some seven years earlier. The sale benefited San Francisco's Silver Street Free Kindergartens. Now she places it in publishers' hands for the first time. At their request she has added new material. The present story runs to over twice the length of the first sketch. She wrote that sketch for charity.
understood-betsy: Dorothy Canfield wrote Understood Betsy, with pictures by Ada C. Williamson. The pages here give the title page, a list of pictures, and a contents list of eleven chapters, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters follow a girl named Elizabeth Ann, called Betsy. Her Aunt Harriet has a cough, and Betsy holds the reins. She goes to school, fails a test, starts a sewing society, and has a birthday. The last chapter is called Understood Aunt Frances.
